title: The Origin of Strawberries
text:
The Cherokee tell that when the first man and the first woman had not been married long, they quarreled. The woman, angry, left the house and set off walking toward the east, toward the Sun, and she did not look back.

The man followed, grieving, but she kept far ahead and would not stop. The Sun took pity on him and asked if he was still angry with his wife. He said he was not. Would he like her to come back? Yes, he said, he would.

So the Sun made a patch of ripe huckleberries spring up along the path in front of the woman. She walked straight past without looking at them. Farther on the Sun put a clump of blackberries beside the way. She ignored those too. The Sun tried other fruits and trees, but nothing tempted her.

At last the Sun made a patch of strawberries grow, the first there had ever been, bright red and sweet. She stopped to pick a few. As she ate, she turned to face the west and began to think of her husband, and she found she could not go on. She sat down and gathered strawberries until he caught up with her. Then they went home together.
lesson: After a fight, walking away is easy, and stopping is the hard part. Something small and sweet, offered in time, can give both people room to turn around.
people: The first man, the first woman, the Sun
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (Nineteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1900), Origin of Strawberries
